A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Uni-X research. Their full text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original Uni-X benchmark results, training-efficiency measurements, ablations, qualitative examples and gradient analyses, including Appendix A.3.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds a larger training condition, image-editing evaluation, further generation benchmarks, inference measurements and additional analyses.

M1.justification: The tokenizer, modality routing, two-end-separated/shared-middle architecture and autoregressive training objective remain unchanged. The new capacity ablations and image-editing results do not document a new algorithmic component or revised editing procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds image editing on ImgEdit-Bench, T2I-CompBench color/shape/texture evaluation, and MSCOCO generation evaluation. Appendix A.4 additionally introduces code/math/wiki diagnostic comparisons and HumanEval/GSM8K testing. These substantially broaden the evaluated tasks and data beyond v1.

E2.justification: The new editing comparison includes GPT-4o, ICEdit, AnyEdit, UltraEdit, Step1X-Edit and Bagel (v2 Table 3). The added generation comparison includes SDXL, Janus and UniToken alongside Liquid and EMU3 (Table 7). The comparator sets in the original experiments are retained.

E3.justification: Section 3.1 replaces the single-minibatch gradient description with averaging over 60-plus minibatches/2M tokens and a baseline using disjoint dataset halves. v2 also adds a 240B-token training condition, zero-shot domain tests, unequal text/vision layer counts, and an inference protocol using batch size 48 and approximately 1,200 input tokens. The revised description does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix A.4 adds cross-domain conflict and transfer checks across Qwen and Llama models (Tables 8–9). Appendix A.6 tests vision-layer capacity relative to 14 separated text layers (Table 11). The original loss-masking, shallow/deep separation and attention-module analyses remain present.

E5.justification: v2 documents batch-averaged gradient estimates intended to reduce noise, replacing v1's single-batch description; Appendix A.4 specifies 2M tokens over 60 batches per dataset. This revises statistical estimation without establishing additional independent training runs. No new confidence-interval or significance-testing practice is specified.

E6.justification: Original results are retained. The added 240B-token condition reports GenEval 83, MMB 62.7 and SEED 59.8, alongside the retained 140B condition's 82, 59.3 and 60.2; these reflect different training budgets. New entries include ImgEdit overall 3.44, T2I average 66.6, MSCOCO CLIP-T 31.8, inference throughput of 910.2 tokens/s, and domain/capacity results.

T1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds an attention-cost derivation comparing a^2+b^2 with (a+b)^2 for modality-separated mixed sequences. The conflict-score formula, entropy expression and architecture/loss equations are retained, although gradient estimation is revised separately.

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims priority in transferring gradient conflict from multitask learning to unified multimodal models. The abstract, three principal contributions and conclusion otherwise retain the same architectural, efficiency and scalability claims.

C2.justification: v2 extends interpretation to positive code/math transfer, semantic unification as an explanation for editing performance, token partitioning and token counts as explanations for inference efficiency, and visual-processing burden as an explanation for text degradation with fewer vision layers. It also newly acknowledges incomplete inference optimization and the absence of specific web-data bias filtering.

D1.justification: v2 adds an anonymous code-access address alongside the retained GitHub address, specifies H800 PCIe 350W inference hardware, clarifies the 28-layer configuration and split points, and discloses the lack of specific bias filtering. Most original implementation details remain unchanged; the new 240B training and editing procedures receive limited documentation.

R1.justification: v2 newly connects its gradient-conflict framing to Gradient Surgery and Recon, with an explicit priority claim for applying the concept to UMMs. It adds references supporting the new benchmarks and domain analysis, including UniToken and DeepSeekMath. The broader related-work survey and architectural positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction receives localized rewriting and the gradient-measurement explanation expands. Ethics and reproducibility statements and additional appendix subsections are added. The abstract, method exposition and overall main-section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a three-panel gradient-conflict illustration and six tables (Tables 3 and 7–11). It restyles the gradient and entropy plots, expands Table 2, and resizes/reflows the in-context examples and configuration table. The original architecture diagram, qualitative examples and attention plots are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 makes the central gradient analysis easier to assess through clearer sampling and averaging documentation, and adds useful capacity and inference checks absent from v1. Broader evaluation strengthens empirical support. The gains are limited by sparse details for the 240B run and image editing, and by causal interpretations that the cross-model comparisons do not isolate.
